reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO / India NTEP
clinicalPearls: Caused by the flagellated protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis and spread almost exclusively through sexual contact, so it should prompt screening for other sexually transmitted infections
Women often present with a malodorous, frothy yellow-green discharge, vulvovaginal itching and dysuria, though a large proportion are asymptomatic
The classic 'strawberry cervix' (punctate cervical haemorrhages) is highly suggestive but seen in only a minority of cases
Most infected men are asymptomatic carriers but may develop urethritis, making partner treatment essential to prevent reinfection
Diagnosis is traditionally by observing motile trophozoites on saline wet mount, but nucleic acid amplification testing is far more sensitive and is now preferred where available
Treatment is with an oral nitroimidazole (metronidazole or tinidazole); partners should be treated simultaneously and intercourse avoided until both complete therapy
Infection in pregnancy is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight, and it increases susceptibility to HIV acquisition and transmission
reference.pathophysiology: Trichomonas vaginalis is an anaerobic, flagellated protozoan that adheres to and damages squamous epithelium of the urogenital tract. Cytoadherence and release of proteinases and other virulence factors trigger a local inflammatory response with neutrophil infiltration, producing the characteristic discharge and mucosal microhaemorrhages. The resulting disruption of the epithelial barrier and mucosal inflammation facilitates acquisition and shedding of HIV and other pathogens. The organism cannot survive long outside a moist environment, which underlies its predominantly sexual mode of transmission.
infectionMimics: Candida vulvovaginitis causing itch and discharge
Chlamydial or gonococcal cervicitis or urethritis
additionalInvestigations: Saline wet-mount microscopy for motile trophozoites and increased polymorphs
Nucleic acid amplification testing of vaginal or urethral specimens as the most sensitive method
Vaginal pH and whiff testing to help distinguish from bacterial vaginosis
Concurrent screening for HIV, syphilis, gonorrhoea and chlamydia
Culture in selective medium where molecular testing is unavailable
redFlags: Infection during pregnancy given the association with preterm delivery and low birth weight
Persistent symptoms after treatment suggesting reinfection or nitroimidazole resistance
Coexisting HIV infection or features suggesting other serious sexually transmitted disease
Signs of pelvic inflammatory disease indicating an alternative or additional pathogen
reference.prognosis: With appropriate nitroimidazole therapy and simultaneous partner treatment the cure rate is high; recurrence usually reflects reinfection or non-adherence rather than true drug resistance, which is uncommon but increasingly recognised.
pitfalls: Relying on wet-mount microscopy alone, which misses many infections because of its limited sensitivity
Treating the index patient without treating sexual partners, leading to reinfection
Overlooking asymptomatic infection, particularly in men, who sustain transmission
Failing to screen for coexisting sexually transmitted infections and HIV
management: Treat with an oral nitroimidazole (metronidazole or tinidazole) as definitive antiprotozoal therapy, counselling on avoidance of alcohol during and shortly after treatment
Treat all recent sexual partners simultaneously and advise abstaining from intercourse until both partners have completed therapy, to prevent reinfection
Screen for and manage coexisting sexually transmitted infections including HIV, syphilis, gonorrhoea and chlamydia
Arrange retesting for cure given the high reinfection rate, and treat symptomatic pregnant women, involving obstetrics for regimen choice
For persistent infection after adherent treatment, use a prolonged or higher-intensity tinidazole-based regimen and seek specialist advice on the uncommon nitroimidazole resistance
Counsel on consistent condom use and safer-sex practices to reduce recurrence and onward transmission
